Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'permanently humiliated' is hard to reconcile unless the illness involved a specifically shaming interpersonal circumstance; nothing else in the profile suggests that context. The other items center danger, fear, vivid reliving, and generalized threat, so humiliation stands out as clinically mismatched to the trauma type.

vignette: John, a 78-year-old North American male and retired Database Administrator, has experienced profound psychological distress following his life-threatening illness. John had always been meticulous about his work and home environment; however, since surviving the near-fatal event, he found himself on constant alert even within the confines of his own home. The fear that something could go wrong again kept him hyper-vigilant, perpetually scanning for signs of danger. The traumatic illness left John with vivid memories that often intruded into his daily life. When he smelled certain odors—like the antiseptic scent from cleaning products—he was immediately transported back to the hospital where he had spent weeks fighting for his life. These smells triggered intense feelings, as if the event were happening all over again. He found it particularly distressing that these memories felt more real and vivid than any other recollections of his past. John's experience with the illness had profoundly affected his view of the world. He now believed that life was fundamentally dangerous and unpredictable, leading him to lose faith in people and a higher power. His body, once seen as a reliable vessel for work and daily activities, now betrayed him by reacting in fear even when he knew he was safe. This discrepancy between rational thought and bodily response often left John feeling trapped in a perpetual state of anxiety. His hypervigilance extended to his workplace during the years before retirement. He found himself constantly worried about another health scare, which made it difficult for him to fully engage with colleagues or tasks that required concentration. Over time, this anxiety led to increased social withdrawal and strained relationships at work. Colleagues who once considered John a reliable team member began to notice his growing detachment and reluctance to participate in group projects. In the months following his illness, John had developed strict routines aimed at minimizing potential threats. He kept his home meticulously clean, often using strong cleaning products to ensure everything was disinfected. However, these efforts only served to exacerbate his olfactory triggers, creating a cycle of increasing fear and avoidance. John’s relationship with his ex-wife also suffered as he struggled to open up about his fears and anxieties. His reluctance to share his experiences led to misunderstandings and further isolation. He had come to believe that no one could truly understand what he was going through, which reinforced his sense of isolation and mistrust in others. Despite the efforts to maintain control over his environment, John found himself increasingly overwhelmed by negative emotions such as fear, anger, guilt, and shame. These feelings were not just fleeting; they permeated his daily life, making it difficult for him to find moments of peace or enjoyment. What finally brought John to seek help was a particularly distressing episode where he experienced a panic attack at a family gathering. The combination of the crowded environment and the strong odors from the food triggered an intense reliving of the traumatic event. This incident made him realize that his current state was not sustainable and that he needed professional support to manage his symptoms. John’s primary fear is that another life-threatening illness will strike again, leaving him vulnerable and isolated once more. He hopes for a way to regain control over his reactions and find peace in his daily life without the constant specter of danger looming over him. He seeks help with a mixture of trepidation and hope, hoping that therapy can provide some relief from the overwhelming sense of threat and anxiety that has dominated his life since the traumatic event.
